newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks new partnership with Latam - adviser.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks new partnership with Latam - adviser.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, who plans to visit South America twice in the next 10 months, is seeking a new partnership with the hemisphere's nations, his top adviser on Latin America said on Tuesday.
Thomas "Mack" McLarty said the Americas II Summit to be held in Chile next April will launch hemispheric free trade negotiations long awaited by Latin American nations.
The plan, however, may hinge on obtaining fast-track negotiating authority from an increasingly protectionist Congress.
"The President believes the time is right for a deepened partnership based on common interests and shared values," McLarty said in an interview at the White House.
With democracy sweeping all of Latin America, except for Cuba, the Clinton administration thinks the United States has an historic opportunity to build a new relationship.
"We want to try to affirm these open market democracies and strengthen democratic institutions," said the former White House chief of staff who is now Clinton's personal envoy for Latin America.

At the first Americas summit in Miami in 1994, Clinton vowed to build free trade across the hemisphere by 2005. Chile was invited to join the North American Free Trade Agreement, but has been waiting ever since as the Clinton administration has not sought fast-track authority from Congress since 1994.
"We are committed to achieving broad fast-track authority and will be introducing legislation to Congress early in September," McLarty said. "I prefer to be optimistic."
He said Chile was the "next logical building block" in the process of creating the Free Trade Area of the Americas, building on top of the NAFTA agreement with Canada and Mexico.
The lifting of a 20-year U.S. ban on the sale of advanced weapons to Latin America, announced on Friday, was a sign of a maturing relationship with Latin America, McLarty said.

The embargo was enforced by the Carter administration at a time when most of the region was under military dictatorships. The policy change will clear the way for countries like Chile to buy F-16 warplanes.
"President Clinton felt our relationships with these democracies should be the same as our relationships with other democracies throughout the world," he said.
The United States will continue its efforts to further isolate Cuba's Communist government in the hope of achieving a peaceful transition to democratic rule on the island, he said.
"While democracy has permeated the region with a clear desire of the people to have a voice in their government, Cuba stands as a very stark exception," he said.

McLarty said the U.S. objectives, if not its tactics, were shared by other Latin American and European allies, and the White House had made progress in patching up differences over the Helms-Burton Law discouraging foreign investment in Cuba.
European Union members had changed their public stance on Cuba and come out with calls for change in Cuba, he said.
McLarty said the U.S. government was discussing the creation of a multinational anti-narcotics force to be based in Panama after the United States hands over control of the canal in 1999.
"This drug centre could require some continued presence of U.S. troops in Panama, but that has not been agreed upon."
Clinton will visit Brazil, Argentina and Venezuela in mid-October.
